prompt.context: Farsung Electronics (FE) is a consumer goods producing company based in the US. During the last couple of years FE has been losing market share to its competitors. The CEO has approached us to help the company tackle the problem of decreasing market share. FE produces home appliances of all types – from dishwashers to irons and frying pans. It has approximately 30% of US market share. The market has been flat during the last couple of years. Competitors haven't seen any remarkable growth. FE has production facilities located in China and the US. Most of the products are produced in China and delivered to the US.
prompt.question: Why is FE losing market share, and what should the company do to address this problem?

clarifying_info.q: What is FE's current revenue and how has it changed?
clarifying_info.a: Revenue has declined from $35B to $28B, a 20% decrease.

clarifying_info.q: Has the overall market size changed?
clarifying_info.a: Market size has remained relatively constant at $100B.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the main competitors and how are they performing?
clarifying_info.a: Competitor 2 has captured a lot of market share from FE. Competitor 3 is the fastest growing – its market share has increased by 50%, with revenues growing from $10B to $15B.
Most products are produced in China and delivered to the US. FE also has production facilities in the US.

exhibits.title: Total Market in $B – Market Size and Market Share
exhibits.shows: A chart showing total market size over time and a breakdown of market share among FE and its competitors across years.
exhibits.data: Total market size ~$100B (flat). FE market share ~30% declining. Competitor 2 and Competitor 3 gaining share.

exhibits.title: Industry vs FE – Price and Cost Trends (2007–2012)
exhibits.shows: Two side-by-side charts: one showing industry average price trend, one showing FE's price trend. Each chart includes a cost and profit breakdown stack.
exhibits.data: Industry average price declined from $300 to $220 (2007–2012). Industry costs stayed at $50 throughout. FE price increased from $300 to $340 (2007–2012). FE costs rose from $50 to $20 profit margin implies costs increased (cost bar grew from $50 to higher levels as profit shrank from $50 to $20).

exhibits.title: China vs US Production – Volume and Demand Volatility
exhibits.shows: A scatter or bubble chart plotting products by volume produced (thousands) on one axis and demand volatility on another, with products grouped by production location (Minnesota, California, China Province Hebei, China Province Shanxi).
exhibits.data: X-axis: Demand Volatility (0%–180%). Y-axis: Volume produced in thousands (0–2500). Products from China provinces (Hebei, Shanxi) appear at higher demand volatility and higher volume. US locations (Minnesota, California) appear at lower volatility and lower volume.

framework: Revenue analysis: examine market share loss – FE revenue down 20% ($35B to $28B) while overall market flat at $100B
Pricing analysis: compare FE pricing vs. industry – investigate whether FE is priced above market
Cost analysis: examine FE cost trends vs. industry cost trends – identify root cause of rising costs
Operations / supply chain: investigate production locations, lead times, inventory, and demand volatility
Competitive dynamics: understand how Competitor 2 and Competitor 3 gained share

questions.prompt: What is the revenue loss for FE and who is gaining market share?
questions.guidance: FE revenue declined from $35B to $28B (a $7B or ~20% decrease). Total market is flat at ~$100B. Competitor 2 has captured significant share from FE; Competitor 3 is the fastest growing with share up 50% (from $10B to $15B in revenue).

math.answer: FE lost $7B (20%) in revenue. Competitor 3 grew 50% from $10B to $15B.

questions.prompt: Looking at pricing trends, what does Exhibit 2 tell us about FE's competitiveness?
questions.guidance: While industry average prices declined from $300 to $220 over 2007–2012 (a ~27% drop), FE's prices rose from $300 to $340. This means FE became significantly more expensive relative to the market. At the same time, FE's costs rose (profit margin shrank from $50 to $20 while revenue per unit went up), meaning cost increases are eroding profitability even as FE charges more. This combination of rising prices and rising costs, while the rest of the industry cut prices, explains why FE is losing market share.

math.setup: Industry price change = ($220 - $300) / $300. FE price change = ($340 - $300) / $300.
steps: FE costs rose: at $300 price with $50 profit, cost = $250; at $340 price with $20 profit, cost = $320; cost increase = ($320 - $250) / $250 = 28%
math.answer: Industry prices fell ~27% while FE prices rose ~13%. FE unit costs rose ~28%, squeezing margin and forcing higher prices.

questions.prompt: What does Exhibit 3 reveal about FE's cost drivers?
questions.guidance: The most volatile products (high demand volatility) are also produced in the highest volumes and are made in China (Hebei and Shanxi provinces). High demand volatility combined with long China-to-US shipping lead times creates two problems: (1) excess inventory is required to buffer against demand uncertainty, driving up inventory and transportation costs; (2) shipping delays can result in lost sales when demand spikes. This explains the rising cost structure seen in Exhibit 2. US-produced products (Minnesota, California) have lower volatility and lower volumes, and thus do not face the same inventory/shipping cost problem.

brainstorming.prompt: What might be causing FE's costs to rise while the rest of the industry is cutting costs?

categories.name: Supply chain / logistics
ideas: Long lead times from China production to US delivery
Shipping delays causing lost sales and emergency re-orders
High safety stock / buffer inventory required due to demand uncertainty
Increasing ocean freight or shipping costs

categories.name: Demand volatility
ideas: High-volume products have volatile demand, making forecasting difficult
Volatile demand forces over-production or under-production
Excess inventory drives warehousing and carrying costs
Stock-outs during demand spikes drive lost revenue

categories.name: Manufacturing
ideas: Rising labor or input costs in China
Inefficient production processes not keeping pace with industry
Exchange rate fluctuations increasing effective cost of China production
Quality issues requiring rework or returns

categories.name: Organizational / structural
ideas: Lack of collaboration with retail buyers on demand forecasting
Slow response to market pricing signals

recommendation: Move production of the highest-volume, most demand-volatile products from China to the US. This will reduce inventory carrying costs (less buffer stock needed), eliminate long trans-Pacific lead times, and prevent lost sales from shipping delays.
risks: Other manufacturing costs (labor, overhead, facilities) will be higher in the US than in China – a full cost comparison is required before committing
Significant capital investment is required to build or expand US manufacturing capacity
Relocation may take significant time, during which FE continues to lose market share
next_steps: Conduct a full analysis of manufacturing costs in the US vs. China for the high-volatility product lines
Negotiate long-term contracts with retail customers to reduce demand volatility
Increase collaboration with retail buyers and integrate a demand forecasting / sales planning system to improve forecast accuracy
Evaluate whether remaining low-volatility products should stay in China
